s0003.literal: Xu Shipu; Lu Xida; Zhou Fu; Xun Lang; son Fashang; Zhou Jiong
s0003.idiomatic: Xu Shipu; Lu Xida; Zhou Fu; Xun Lang; son Fashang; Zhou Jiong

s0005.literal: Xu Shipu, styled Xingzong, was a native of Yufu in Badong.
s0005.idiomatic: Xu Shipu, styled Xingzong, came from Yufu in Badong.

s0006.literal: For generations the family dwelt in Jingzhou as a territorial commander, campaigning against the Man and the Yi.
s0006.idiomatic: His clan had long held Jingzhou as local commanders, campaigning against the Man and Yi peoples.

s0007.literal: By Shipu's time he was especially daring and brave, with great physical strength, and skilled in naval warfare.
s0007.idiomatic: Shipu was bolder and stronger than his forebears and excelled at river fighting.

s0008.literal: When Emperor Yuan of Liang was governor of Jingzhou, Shipu led the local commanders and village heads in serving him.
s0008.idiomatic: When Emperor Yuan of Liang governed Jingzhou, Shipu led the district commanders and village heads in his service.

s0009.literal: In Hou Jing's rebellion he took part in the punitive campaigns and rose in succession to supernumerary scattered-cavalry regular attendant.
s0009.idiomatic: In Hou Jing's rebellion he joined the punitive armies and rose step by step to supernumerary scattered-cavalry regular attendant.

s0010.literal: Soon he took command of the navy and, following Minister of Education Lu Fahe, campaigned against Jing, fighting him at Red Pavilion Lake.
s0010.idiomatic: Soon he commanded the navy and, under Minister of Education Lu Fahe, marched against Jing and fought him at Red Pavilion Lake.

s0011.literal: At that time Jing's army was very strong; Shipu thereupon had tower ships, battering ships, fire vessels, and water-wheels built separately to strengthen the fleet.
s0011.idiomatic: Jing's army was then overwhelming. Shipu had new tower ships, rams, fire-boats, and water-engines built to swell his fleet.

s0012.literal: As battle was joined he again took a great war-ship to the fore, inflicted a great defeat on Jing's army, captured Jing's general Ren Yue alive, and Jing fled.
s0012.idiomatic: When battle came he again put a great ship in the van, crushed Jing's army, took Jing's general Ren Yue alive, and drove Jing off.

s0013.literal: He then followed Wang Sengbian in attacking Yingzhou; Shipu again took a great war-ship up to the granary gate, and the rebel general Song Zixian surrendered the city.
s0013.idiomatic: He followed Wang Sengbian against Yingzhou. Shipu again brought a great ship under the granary gate, and the rebel Song Zixian surrendered the city.

s0014.literal: For merit he was appointed holder of credentials, trustworthy-faith general, and inspector of Xinzhou, enfeoffed as Marquis of Yufu county with a fief of five hundred households.
s0014.idiomatic: For merit he was made credential-holder, trustworthy-faith general, and inspector of Xinzhou, enfeoffed as Marquis of Yufu with five hundred households.

s0015.literal: He still followed Sengbian eastward, always serving as the army's vanguard.
s0015.idiomatic: He still marched east with Sengbian and was always the army's vanguard.

s0016.literal: He again defeated Jing's general Hou Zijian at Hushu.
s0016.idiomatic: He again broke Jing's general Hou Zijian at Hushu.

s0017.literal: Editorial footnote marker 1. After Hou Jing was pacified, for merit he was appointed regular attendant for direct communication, with credentials as inspector of Hengzhou,
s0017.idiomatic: [1] After Hou Jing fell, for merit he was made regular attendant for direct communication and given credentials as inspector of Hengzhou,

s0019.literal: [garrison] Administrator of Hedong, Editorial footnote marker 2. fief increased to one thousand households combined with the former.
s0019.idiomatic: [garrison] administrator of Hedong, [2] with his fief raised to one thousand households in all.

s0020.literal: Western Wei came to raid Jingzhou; Shipu garrisoned Matou Bank and held Long
s0020.idiomatic: When Western Wei raided Jingzhou, Shipu held Matou Bank and occupied Long

s0022.literal: [Islet], Editorial footnote marker 3. Emperor Yuan appointed him palace attendant, credential-holder, area commander of all armies south of the Yangzi, general who guards the south, protector-general, and gave him one set of pipes and drums.
s0022.idiomatic: [Islet]. [3] Emperor Yuan made him palace attendant, credential-holder, commander of all armies south of the Yangzi, general who guards the south, and protector-general, with one set of pipes and drums.

s0023.literal: When Jiangling fell, Shipu went east and attached himself to Hou Zhen.
s0023.idiomatic: When Jiangling fell, Shipu went east and joined Hou Zhen.

s0024.literal: In the second year of Yongding he was transferred to protector-general.
s0024.idiomatic: In Yongding year 2 (558) he was made protector-general.

s0025.literal: When Emperor Wen succeeded to the throne, he was given special advance and promoted to secure-the-right general.
s0025.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen succeeded, he was given special advance and promoted to secure-the-right general.

s0026.literal: In the first year of Tiancheng his fief was increased by five hundred households.
s0026.idiomatic: In Tiancheng year 1 (560) his fief grew by five hundred households.

s0027.literal: In the second year he went out with credentials as supernumerary scattered-cavalry regular attendant, area commander of all military affairs in Xuancheng prefecture, secure-the-west general, and administrator of Xuancheng, salary at the two-thousand-bushel level.
s0027.idiomatic: In the second year he went out as credential-holder, supernumerary scattered-cavalry regular attendant, commander of armies in Xuancheng, secure-the-west general, and administrator of Xuancheng at the two-thousand-bushel rank.

s0028.literal: Returning, he was made secure-the-front general and supernumerary bearer of the left secondary insignia.
s0028.idiomatic: Back at court he was made secure-the-front general and supernumerary bearer of the left secondary insignia.

s0029.literal: Soon he went blind from illness and excused himself from court on grounds of illness.
s0029.idiomatic: Soon illness blinded him, and he begged leave from court.

s0030.literal: In the fourth year he died, aged fifty-five.
s0030.idiomatic: In the fourth year he died, aged fifty-five.

s0031.literal: He was posthumously given his former offices; posthumous name Marquis Huan.
s0031.idiomatic: He was posthumously given his former offices, with the posthumous name Marquis Huan.

s0032.literal: Shipu's younger cousin Shiuxiu followed Shipu on Liang punitive campaigns and also had battle merit.
s0032.idiomatic: Shipu's younger cousin Shiuxiu followed him on Liang campaigns and won merit in battle.

s0033.literal: He rose to supernumerary scattered-cavalry regular attendant and secure-the-distance general, Marquis of Zhi county with a fief of eight hundred households.
s0033.idiomatic: He rose to supernumerary scattered-cavalry regular attendant and secure-the-distance general, Marquis of Zhi with eight hundred households.

s0034.literal: In the second year of Guangda he served under Area Commander Chunyu Liang in campaigning against Hua Jiao.
s0034.idiomatic: In Guangda year 2 (567) he served under area commander Chunyu Liang against Hua Jiao.

s0035.literal: When he died he was posthumously given regular attendant for direct communication; posthumous name Zhuang.
s0035.idiomatic: When he died he was posthumously made regular attendant for direct communication, with the posthumous name Zhuang.

s0037.literal: Lu Xida, styled Zhitong, was a native of Mei in Fufeng.
s0037.idiomatic: Lu Xida, styled Zhitong, came from Mei in Fufeng.

s0038.literal: His grandfather Fei was Liang supernumerary regular attendant for direct communication, secure-the-distance general, inspector of Hengzhou, and Marquis of Yangtang.
s0038.idiomatic: His grandfather Fei was Liang's supernumerary regular attendant for direct communication, secure-the-distance general, inspector of Hengzhou, and Marquis of Yangtang.

s0039.literal: His father Yizhi was Liang cloud-banner general and concurrently administrator of the two commanderies of Xincai and Yiyang.
s0039.idiomatic: His father Yizhi was Liang's cloud-banner general and concurrently administrator of Xincai and Yiyang.

s0040.literal: From youth Xida was famed for filial piety; he first took office as army supervisor in the establishment of the Prince of Southern Pacification, heir of Liang's Prince of Nangping.
s0040.idiomatic: From boyhood Xida was known for filial piety. He first entered service as army supervisor in the establishment of the Prince of Southern Pacification, heir to Liang's Prince of Nangping.

s0041.literal: In Hou Jing's rebellion Xida gathered fellow-townsmen to hold Xincai, farming diligently and storing grain.
s0041.idiomatic: In Hou Jing's rebellion Xida rallied his neighbors to hold Xincai, farmed hard, and stored grain.

s0042.literal: In that time of military chaos and famine, nine or ten in the capital and upper Yangzi valley died of hunger; those who survived all brought the aged and young back with them.
s0042.idiomatic: In the war and famine, eight or nine of ten in the capital and upper Yangzi died of hunger. Those who lived came back with the old and young in tow.

s0043.literal: Xida distributed grain from his granaries; those he saved were very many, and he then established a camp at Xincai to house them.
s0043.idiomatic: Xida opened his granaries. The people he kept alive were countless, and he set a camp at Xincai to shelter them.

s0044.literal: He recruited the five commanderies including Jinxi and held all their territory.
s0044.idiomatic: He drew in five commanderies, including Jinxi, and held all their lands.

s0045.literal: He had his younger brother Guangda lead troops to follow Wang Sengbian in suppressing Hou Jing.
s0045.idiomatic: He sent his younger brother Guangda with troops to follow Wang Sengbian against Hou Jing.

s0046.literal: When Jing was pacified Emperor Yuan of Liang appointed him credential-holder, benevolent-martial general, supernumerary scattered-cavalry regular attendant, and inspector of North Jiangzhou.
s0046.idiomatic: When Jing fell, Emperor Yuan of Liang made him credential-holder, benevolent-martial general, supernumerary scattered-cavalry regular attendant, and inspector of North Jiangzhou.

s0047.literal: Though Xida relied on qi and was a knight-errant, he was not proud in wealth and rank; he loved rhapsodies and poems by nature and recruited and treated men of talent, sharing appreciation with them.
s0047.idiomatic: Though he lived by bold spirit and the code of the knight-errant, he was never haughty in wealth or rank. He loved verse by nature, gathered men of talent, and feasted with them on their writing.

s0048.literal: He was transferred to secure-the-south general and inspector of Wu prefecture.
s0048.idiomatic: He was transferred to secure-the-south general and inspector of Wu prefecture.

s0049.literal: He encountered mourning for his mother; his grief and emaciation exceeded ritual, and he thereupon fell ill and died, aged thirty-eight.
s0049.idiomatic: When his mother died his grief and wasting went beyond ritual. He fell ill and died, aged thirty-eight.

s0050.literal: Posthumously he was given secure-the-left general and inspector of Jiangzhou; posthumous name Marquis Xiao.
s0050.idiomatic: Posthumously he was made secure-the-left general and inspector of Jiangzhou, with the posthumous name Marquis Xiao.

s0052.literal: His younger brother Guangda has a separate biography.
s0052.idiomatic: His younger brother Guangda has a separate biography.

s0053.literal: Zhou Fu, styled Zhongyuan, was a native of Linchuan.
s0053.idiomatic: Zhou Fu, styled Zhongyuan, came from Linchuan.

s0054.literal: His clan was a great family of the commandery.
s0054.idiomatic: His clan was a great house of the commandery.

s0055.literal: Fu's looks were slight and small, as if he could not bear his clothes, yet his courage and strength were fierce and resolute, surpassing men of the time.
s0055.idiomatic: Fu was slight of build, as if his clothes weighed him down, yet his courage and force were fierce, beyond his peers.

s0056.literal: By nature he was bold and chivalrous, light with wealth and heavy with scholars; young men of the village who trusted in bold spirit all joined him.
s0056.idiomatic: He was bold and chivalrous by nature, careless of money and devoted to men of worth. Every hot-blooded youth in the district rallied to him.

s0057.literal: In Hou Jing's rebellion the townsman Zhou Xu gathered a host under the name of suppressing bandits; Liang's interior secretary the Prince of Shixing Xiao Yi made over the commandery to Xu, Editorial footnote marker 6. and within Xu's command some wished to plunder Yi; Fu guarded him, personally leading his faction to defend and escort him to Yuzhang.
s0057.idiomatic: In Hou Jing's rebellion the townsman Zhou Xu raised men in the name of punishing rebels. Liang's interior secretary, Prince of Shixing Xiao Yi, yielded the commandery to Xu. [6] Some of Xu's men meant to plunder Yi. Fu shielded him, led his own band in defense, and saw him safely to Yuzhang.

s0058.literal: At that time the Marquis of Guanning Xiao Yong, the Marquis of Changle Xiao Ji, and the Marquis of Fengcheng Xiao Tai were refugees in flight; hearing of Fu's trustworthiness and righteousness they all went to rely on him.
s0058.idiomatic: The Marquis of Guanning Xiao Yong, the Marquis of Changle Xiao Ji, and the Marquis of Fengcheng Xiao Tai were then refugees. Hearing of Fu's faith and honor, they all came to him.

s0059.literal: Fu pitied their peril and fear, bowed his body in reverence, gave them generous relief, and sent them upriver west.
s0059.idiomatic: Fu pitied their fear, treated them with humble courtesy, gave them generous aid, and sent them west upriver.

s0060.literal: Before long Xu's subordinate commanders vied for power, rebelled again, killed Xu, and surrendered to Zhou Di.
s0060.idiomatic: Soon Xu's officers fought for power, rebelled again, killed Xu, and submitted to Zhou Di.

s0061.literal: Di by nature had no register of lineage and feared losing the hearts of the masses; relying on Fu's clan prestige he sought his friendship deeply.
s0061.idiomatic: Di had no pedigree in the registers and feared losing the crowd. He leaned on Fu's family standing and courted him hard.

s0062.literal: Fu could not yet secure himself and served Di with great deference; Di leaned heavily on him and gradually had troops and horses.
s0062.idiomatic: Fu could not yet stand alone and served Di with deep deference. Di relied on him heavily and slowly built an army.

s0063.literal: Di held Gongtang in Linchuan; Fu garrisoned the old commandery seat of Linchuan.
s0063.idiomatic: Di held Gongtang in Linchuan; Fu held the old commandery seat.

s0064.literal: When Jing was pacified Emperor Yuan of Liang appointed Fu credential-holder, regular attendant for direct communication, trustworthy-faith general, and inspector of Ningzhou, enfeoffed as Marquis of Xifeng county with a fief of one thousand households.
s0064.idiomatic: When Jing fell, Emperor Yuan of Liang made Fu credential-holder, regular attendant for direct communication, trustworthy-faith general, and inspector of Ningzhou, enfeoffed as Marquis of Xifeng with one thousand households.

s0065.literal: When the Founder received the abdication, Wang Lin held the upper Yangzi; Yu Xiaoxiang with Lin's partisan Li
s0065.idiomatic: When the Founder took the throne, Wang Lin held the upper Yangzi. Yu Xiaoxiang with Lin's ally Li

s0067.literal: [Xiao] Qin and others jointly besieged Zhou Di, Editorial footnote marker 7. and Fu gathered a great force of men and horses to aid Di.
s0067.idiomatic: [Xiao] Qin and others besieged Zhou Di together. [7] Fu mustered a great body of men and horses to help Di.

s0068.literal: Di captured Xiaoxiang and the others; Fu's merit was greatest.
s0068.idiomatic: Di took Xiaoxiang and his fellows prisoner. Fu's share of the merit was greatest.

s0069.literal: Xiong Tanlang killed Zhou Wenyü, held Yuzhang, and with more than ten thousand troops raided Fu, coming straight to the foot of the walls; Fu fought him and inflicted a great defeat, pursued more than fifty li; Tanlang escaped on a single horse and all his military stores were taken.
s0069.idiomatic: Xiong Tanlang killed Zhou Wenyü, held Yuzhang, and struck Fu with more than ten thousand men, coming straight to the walls. Fu fought him, routed him, and chased him fifty li. Tanlang escaped on one horse; all his stores fell to Fu.

s0070.literal: Tanlang fled to Bashan commandery and gathered the remnant party; Fu then with Zhou Di, Huang Faqu, and others advanced to surround Tanlang and slaughtered them.
s0070.idiomatic: Tanlang fled to Bashan commandery and rallied the remnants. Fu then marched with Zhou Di, Huang Faqu, and others, surrounded Tanlang, and slaughtered his force.

s0071.literal: When Wang Lin was pacified he was appointed supernumerary scattered-cavalry regular attendant, pacifying-the-west general, and administrator of Yuzhang.
s0071.idiomatic: When Wang Lin fell he was made supernumerary scattered-cavalry regular attendant, pacifying-the-west general, and administrator of Yuzhang.

s0072.literal: At that time southern river chieftains all clung to their nests and caves, privately appointing magistrates and heads and not answering summonses; the court had not yet leisure to punish them but only kept them on leashes—only Fu alone first entered court.
s0072.idiomatic: Southern chieftains still clung to their hill nests, appointing their own magistrates and ignoring summons. The court had no leisure to punish them and could only hold them on a loose rein—only Fu came to court first.

s0073.literal: In the second year of Tiancheng he came to the palace; his title was advanced to secure-the-west general and he was given one set of pipes and drums and a set of female musicians, Editorial footnote marker 8. with orders to return and hold Yuzhang.
s0073.idiomatic: In Tiancheng year 2 (561) he came to the capital. His title rose to secure-the-west general; he was given pipes and drums and a troupe of female musicians, [8] and ordered back to hold Yuzhang.

s0074.literal: Zhou Di because Fu had always ranked below him yet now surged to high honor was deeply resentful; he thereupon raised troops in rebellion and sent his younger brother Fangxing with an army to raid Fu.
s0074.idiomatic: Zhou Di had always outranked Fu, and Fu's sudden rise bred deep resentment. Di rebelled and sent his brother Fangxing to raid Fu.

s0075.literal: Fu fought him and inflicted a great defeat on Fangxing.
s0075.idiomatic: Fu met him in battle and broke Fangxing completely.

s0076.literal: He then led his host to follow Area Commander Wu Mingche in attacking Di, routed him, and captured his younger brother Fangxing together with the various chieftains.
s0076.idiomatic: He then followed area commander Wu Mingche against Di, routed him, and took Fangxing and the other chieftains prisoner.

s0077.literal: An edict made Fu secure-the-west general and administrator of Linchuan; the rest unchanged.
s0077.idiomatic: An edict made him secure-the-west general and administrator of Linchuan; his other honors stood.

s0078.literal: Soon he was summoned with credentials as area commander of military affairs in the two provinces of South Yu and North Jiang, general who guards the south, and inspector of South Yu, fief increased by five hundred households; regular attendant and pipes and drums unchanged.
s0078.idiomatic: Soon he was summoned as credential-holder, commander of armies in South Yu and North Jiang, general who guards the south, and inspector of South Yu, with five hundred more households. His attendant rank and pipes and drums were unchanged.

s0079.literal: In the fifth year Di again gathered remnant masses and returned to raid Dongxing.
s0079.idiomatic: In the fifth year Di rallied his remnants and struck Dongxing again.

s0080.literal: Emperor Wen sent Area Commander Zhang Zhaoda to campaign against Di; Fu again followed the army.
s0080.idiomatic: Emperor Wen sent area commander Zhang Zhaoda against Di, and Fu marched again.

s0081.literal: Reaching Dingchuan county, he faced Di across the line.
s0081.idiomatic: At Dingchuan county he faced Di across the line.

s0082.literal: Di deceived Fu, saying: "Formerly I and you, my younger brother, strove together with one heart; we are clan kin and no others—how could I scheme to harm you?
s0082.idiomatic: Di tricked Fu, saying: "Once we fought side by side, you and I, as kin and not strangers. How could I mean you harm?

s0083.literal: Now I wish to confess guilt and return to court; through you, younger brother, I disclose my inmost heart; first I beg to bare my body and stand together to swear an oath."
s0083.idiomatic: Now I wish to confess and return to court. Through you, younger brother, I lay bare my heart. First let us stand together and swear an oath."

s0084.literal: Fu agreed; as he was mounting the altar he was killed by Di, aged thirty-five.
s0084.idiomatic: Fu agreed. As he climbed the altar, Di killed him. He was thirty-five.

s0085.literal: An edict said: "Credential-holder, supernumerary scattered-cavalry regular attendant, area commander of all armies along the Yangzi bank of South Yu, general who guards the south, inspector of South Yu, Opening Marquis of Xifeng county Fu—charged with a distant expedition, he long disobeyed regulations, held an empty breast toward treacherous deceit, and so met death and fell.
s0085.idiomatic: An edict said: "Fu, credential-holder, supernumerary scattered-cavalry regular attendant, commander of armies along the South Yu Yangzi bank, general who guards the south, inspector of South Yu, and Opening Marquis of Xifeng—sent on a distant campaign, he long broke discipline, opened his heart to treachery, and so met death in the field.

s0086.literal: Editorial footnote marker 9. Yet from of old he showed loyal earnestness and repeatedly labored on campaign; We are still deeply moved to compassion and grieve in Our heart.
s0086.idiomatic: [9] Yet he had long shown loyal service and toil on campaign. We are still deeply moved and grieve in Our heart.

s0087.literal: His feudal income may be preserved; measure out funeral gifts as due and return his body for burial in the capital."
s0087.idiomatic: Let his fief be kept. Give funeral gifts as fitting and bring his body back for burial in the capital."

s0090.literal: Fu's elder brother Juan together with Fu held their home district and was also appointed administrator of Linchuan.
s0090.idiomatic: Fu's elder brother Juan had held their home district with him and was also made administrator of Linchuan.

s0091.literal: Xun Lang, styled Shenming, was a native of Yingyin in Yingchuan.
s0091.idiomatic: Xun Lang, styled Shenming, came from Yingyin in Yingchuan.

s0092.literal: His grandfather Yan'zu was Liang administrator of Yingchuan; his father Bodao was minister of court ceremony.
s0092.idiomatic: His grandfather Yan'zu was Liang's administrator of Yingchuan; his father Bodao was minister of court ceremony.

s0093.literal: From youth Lang was generous and bold, with the grand strategy of a commander; he first took office as traveling attendant in the establishment of Liang's Prince of Luling.
s0093.idiomatic: From youth Lang was open-handed and bold, with a commander's breadth of plan. He first served as traveling attendant in the establishment of Liang's Prince of Luling.

s0094.literal: In Hou Jing's rebellion Lang gathered a following, held the lands about Chaohu Lake, and belonged to no one.
s0094.idiomatic: In Hou Jing's rebellion Lang gathered followers, held the country about Chaohu Lake, and owed allegiance to no one.

s0095.literal: After the Terrace City fell Emperor Jianwen of Liang sent a secret edict appointing Lang cloud-banner general and inspector of Yu and ordering him with outer provinces to suppress Jing.
s0095.idiomatic: After the capital fell, Emperor Jianwen of Liang secretly made him cloud-banner general and inspector of Yu and ordered him, with the outer provinces, to crush Jing.

s0096.literal: Jing sent comrades-in-arms Song Zixian, Ren Yue, and others repeatedly to campaign against him; Lang held mountain stockades in defense and Zixian could not overcome him.
s0096.idiomatic: Jing sent his comrades Song Zixian, Ren Yue, and others against him again and again. Lang held mountain forts and Zixian could not take him.

s0097.literal: At that time the capital had great famine; commoners all went south of the Yangzi to seek food; Lang further recruited followers, doffed his own garments and shared food, giving mutual relief, until his following reached tens of thousands.
s0097.idiomatic: The capital was starving. People crossed the Yangzi to find food. Lang gathered more men, stripped off his own clothes to feed them, and built a following of tens of thousands.

s0098.literal: When Hou Jing was defeated at Baling Lang came out from Ruru Ford to intercept Jing and broke his rearguard.
s0098.idiomatic: When Hou Jing was beaten at Baling, Lang came out from Ruru Ford, cut Jing off, and smashed his rearguard.

s0099.literal: Wang Sengbian campaigned east; Lang sent his general Fan Baosheng and his younger brother Xiao each to lead two thousand troops to assist.
s0099.idiomatic: When Wang Sengbian marched east, Lang sent his general Fan Baosheng and his younger brother Xiao, each with two thousand men, to help.

s0100.literal: After Hou Jing was pacified he again separately defeated Qi general Guo Yuanjian at Chichu Mountain.
s0100.idiomatic: After Hou Jing fell he again defeated Qi general Guo Yuanjian at Chichu Mountain.
